PART 1: NARRATION READY
Let's walk through what your BNR transformer's field is telling us this June. The good news first: the MPTS investment you've already made is working. When this field reaches full optimization, power factor locks at 99.5% flat — perfectly consistent across every load condition across the entire month. Reactive demand drops from a 692-kilovar average down to 133 kilovars. And you recover nearly 239 kilovolt-amperes of transformer headroom that your infrastructure was previously consuming just to circulate reactive energy. Those are real, tangible gains from the investment already in the ground. Now here's the gap we're still working to close. Right now, in the baseline operating condition, BNR is running at 89.7% power factor. Peak demand hits 1,515 kilowatts, and your reactive peak reaches 730 kilovars. The annual waste estimate on this field runs approximately $274,706 per year in direct reactive losses — and when you add the thermal burden and cooling overhead on top of that, the total wasted figure reaches approximately $449,367 per year. That's the optimization target. Your voltage picture adds another layer. The average across June is 476.5 volts — which is already below your 480-volt nominal. And we documented a full zero-volt collapse event, plus recurring voltage dips throughout the month tied to motor starts and refrigeration cycling. That sub-nominal voltage environment puts real cumulative stress on motor windings, drive electronics, and process controls. Four to five outage events also appear in the data — brief in duration, but each one carries cold-chain implications your operations team knows well. The thermal burden reads 602,911 BTU per hour. Your cooling system is drawing 88.4 kilowatts just to manage the heat this reactive field is generating inside your electrical infrastructure. The optimization path is clear. The MPTS system is tuned and achieving the correction the simulation targets — the work now is confirming full coverage across all operating hours and addressing the remaining voltage and harmonic gaps. ---

PART 2: EXECUTIVE SHORT
Here's the short version of where BNR stands in June. Your MPTS is delivering. Full optimization brings power factor to 99.5% flat, cuts reactive demand by roughly 560 kilovars on average, and frees 239 kilovolt-amperes of transformer headroom. Those gains are confirmed in the tuned simulation view — and they're real. The gap that remains is visible in the baseline numbers. Power factor sits at 89.7% in the unoptimized condition. Reactive burden averages 692 kilovars, peaking at 730. Annual waste estimates approximately $275,000 in reactive losses, reaching roughly $449,000 total when thermal burden and cooling overhead are included. Your thermal reading is 602,911 BTU per hour — and your cooling system is drawing 88.4 kilowatts to manage it. The voltage picture shows sub-nominal operation — 476.5-volt average against a 480-volt target — with recurring triangular dips tied to motor starts and four to five brief outage events across the month. In a cold-chain environment, those interruptions matter operationally beyond their electrical duration. Harmonic distortion peaks at 11.4% iTHD — above IEEE 519 thresholds. The MPTS reduces that meaningfully, but a dedicated harmonic audit on the highest-contributing loads would close the remaining gap. The optimization path is defined. Reactive coverage, voltage support timing, and harmonic mitigation are the three levers. The investment is in place — it's a matter of tuning what's there and filling the remaining gaps. ---

PART 3: ENGINEERING DETAILED
Let me give you the full engineering picture on BNR's June field. Start with what the investment is already delivering. The tuned simulation view — which represents the MPTS operating at full optimization across BNR's actual load profile — shows a 99.5% power factor that holds flat from minimum to maximum across the entire 30-day period. That flatness matters. It's not an average that masks excursions — it's a field held consistently corrected across all load conditions. Reactive demand in that optimized state averages 133 kilovars, down from a baseline of 692 kilovars. At the peak, reactive demand drops from 730 kilovars to 152 kilovars. That's a 578-kilovar reduction at the worst-case load moment — the exact moment when reactive burden causes the most thermal stress and the most apparent power waste. The transformer headroom recovery that comes with that correction is 238.9 kilovolt-amperes. Your baseline apparent power averages 1,571 kVA against a 1,605 kVA target ceiling — you're operating with almost no margin. Post-optimization, apparent power compresses to 1,333 kVA. That 239 kVA of recovered headroom is infrastructure capacity available for production growth or reliability margin, without a transformer upgrade. Now let's talk about the optimization gap — the distance between where the baseline currently sits and where the MPTS is designed to take it. In the TBT baseline condition, power factor sits at 89.7%. That means a meaningful fraction of every kilovolt-ampere your utility sees on this transformer is reactive — circulating, non-productive current that heats conductors and windings, stresses transformer insulation, and shows up on your utility bill as demand charges. The annual reactive waste estimate is approximately $274,706. Total wasted — adding thermal burden and cooling overhead — reaches approximately $449,367 per year. That is the full cost of the optimization gap, quantified. The thermal burden reading of 602,911 BTU per hour is a serious number. At that heat load, transformer insulation aging is accelerated. The well-documented engineering principle here is that sustained excess heat above design operating temperature roughly halves insulation service life for every 10 degrees Celsius of elevation. Your cooling system is drawing 88.4 kilowatts at $17.55 per hour to manage that heat — and that cooling cost compresses directly as the reactive field tightens. The current profile from the TM view shows a peak of 1,961 amps — a significant conductor loading that compounds thermal generation throughout the distribution system feeding BNR's loads.

**BNR Transformer | June 2026 — Voltage Stability Findings**

The BNR voltage field for June carries a documented average of 476.5 volts — that is nominally below the 480-volt line-to-line reference — with a measured maximum of 489.2 volts and a confirmed minimum of 0.0 volts. The 0.0-volt minimum is not a meter anomaly; it represents a full voltage collapse event, consistent with a site power interruption captured in the TV view and corroborated by the gold outage streaks visible in the TBT chart body.

Voltage stability behavior across the 30-day period is characterized by recurring triangular drop patterns distributed throughout the month. These are not clustered into a single fault window — they appear across the full dataset, which is the signature of process-driven load events rather than isolated equipment failures. The drop profile — sharp descent, brief trough, recovery — is consistent with large inductive motor starts and refrigeration compression cycling, both expected in a food processing and cold storage environment.

The blue voltage trace makes repeated excursions toward and below the 480-volt nominal line during load events. Given that the operating average is already 476.5 volts, these dips push portions of the facility into voltage territory where motor windings, drive electronics, and contactors experience measurable stress. In an operation this load-dense, sustained sub-nominal voltage accelerates insulation degradation and increases nuisance trip probability on sensitive process controls — compressors, PLC-driven conveyors, and CIP (clean-in-place) systems all carry voltage sensitivity that this profile challenges.

The outage picture adds another layer: approximately 4 to 5 distinct gold-streak events are visible in the TBT chart, each estimated at 1 to 2 minutes in duration, totaling roughly 5 to 10 minutes of site power interruption across June. In a cold-chain food processing environment, even a 2-minute outage carries product safety and process restart implications that go well beyond the electrical cost of the event itself.

The MPTS field stabilization captured in the TS view shows improved voltage envelope consistency — the correction system is actively supporting the field — but the voltage dip pattern and sub-nominal average indicate that the full stabilization benefit has not yet been uniformly achieved across all load conditions.

**BNR Transformer | June 2026 — Reactive and Harmonic Findings**

The BNR reactive field in June carries a substantial burden. The TBT header documents a reactive average of 692.6 kVAR, with the operative pre-correction peak reaching 730.8 kVAR. At 89.7% power factor, roughly 44 cents of every dollar of apparent power drawn by this transformer is doing electrical work — the remaining fraction is circulating reactive energy that the utility sees, meters, and charges for, but that delivers no productive output to the facility's processes.

The M view (TM) adds important detail to this picture. The amperage band peaks at 1,961.1 amps — a significant current load that contributes directly to the 602,911 BTU per hour thermal burden. The reactive KVAR band in the M view holds at a consistent elevated level with a Max Reactive reading of 683 kVAR, confirming the reactive burden is persistent rather than event-driven. This is a steady-state condition, not a transient surge profile.

The harmonic content reading from the TM header shows an average iTHD (total harmonic distortion of current) of 6.3%, with a peak iTHD of 11.4%. The 11.4% peak is a meaningful threshold — it exceeds the IEEE 519 standard's recommended limits for many industrial service categories. Harmonic current at this level contributes to transformer heating, increases neutral conductor loading, and degrades the accuracy and lifespan of power measurement instrumentation. In a facility running variable frequency drives, soft starters, and switch-mode power supplies — all common in food processing environments — this distributed harmonic profile is expected, but it still demands managed attention.

The TS view shows what full reactive correction delivers: average kVAR drops to 133.1, peak kVAR drops to 152.1, and apparent power compresses from 1,571.8 kVA to 1,332.9 kVA — freeing 238.9 kVA of transformer capacity. Power factor locks at 99.5% flat. Average iTHD improves from 6.3% to 5.0%. These are the gains the MPTS investment is positioned to deliver when fully optimized across all operating conditions.

---
BNR.operational_stress_interpretation:
**BNR Transformer | June 2026 — Operational Stress Interpretation**

Taken together, the voltage, reactive, and harmonic profiles documented for BNR in June paint a picture of a facility operating under layered and compounding electromagnetic stress — stress that the existing MPTS investment is actively working to reduce, but has not yet fully resolved.

The thermal burden of 602,911 BTU per hour is the most immediate operational consequence. Transformer cores and windings operating at elevated thermal levels experience accelerated insulation aging on a well-documented exponential curve — every 10°C of sustained excess temperature roughly halves insulation service life. The 88.4 kilowatts of cooling load at $17.55 per hour is not just a utility line item; it is the facility's mechanical response to heat that the reactive field is generating inside the electrical infrastructure.

The voltage profile compounds this stress. An operating average of 476.5 volts — below the 480-volt nominal — combined with recurring triangular voltage drops during load cycling means that motors, drives, and contactors at this facility are routinely exposed to sub-nominal conditions. Motor torque output drops roughly as the square of voltage reduction. At 476.5 volts average, that translates to motors working harder to deliver rated torque — drawing more current, generating more heat, and wearing faster than their design life assumes.

The 11.4% peak iTHD harmonic content adds a third stress layer. Harmonic currents cause additional transformer core losses, increase winding temperatures beyond what fundamental-frequency load alone would produce, and create voltage distortion that ripples into sensitive control systems. In a food processing environment where process continuity is a product safety requirement — not just an efficiency preference — harmonic-driven instability in control systems represents real operational risk.

The 4 to 5 outage events observed across June, totaling an estimated 5 to 10 minutes, may appear minor in aggregate duration, but in cold-chain operations each interruption triggers restart protocols, product temperature monitoring reviews, and potential hold events on product batches. The operational cost of these interruptions exceeds the electrical cost by a significant multiple.

The MPTS system already deployed is demonstrably cutting into this stress profile — the TS outcome shows what full optimization looks like — but the gap between the TBT baseline condition and the TS target outcome represents real, ongoing operational exposure that rewards continued attention.

BNR.recommended_engineering_attention_areas:
**BNR Transformer | June 2026 — Recommended Engineering Attention Areas**

Given that BNR is an invested, tuned field still showing a meaningful gap between its TBT baseline and TS optimized outcome, the following engineering attention areas are recommended for the next optimization cycle:

**1. Reactive compensation coverage audit.** The 559.5 kVAR average reduction between TBT and TS represents the full correction target. Confirm that installed MPTS assets are actively compensating at rated capacity across all operating hours — particularly during peak refrigeration and motor-start load cycles. Any derating, scheduling gap, or partial deployment is directly visible in the TBT-versus-TS spread.

**2. Voltage stabilization review for sub-nominal conditions.** The 476.5-volt operating average and recurring triangular drop pattern indicate that voltage support during inductive load events is not yet fully resolved. A targeted review of MPTS capacitor bank switching response time relative to motor-start ramp rates is warranted — faster reactive injection during large motor starts would reduce the depth and frequency of the triangular voltage excursions documented in the TV view.

**3. Harmonic content monitoring and mitigation assessment.** The 11.4% peak iTHD exceeds IEEE 519 thresholds for this industrial service category. With the MPTS already reducing iTHD from 6.3% to 5.0% average, the remaining harmonic content warrants a dedicated harmonic audit — identifying the primary harmonic-generating loads (VFDs, soft starters, rectifier-fed drives) and evaluating whether passive harmonic filters or active front-end drive replacements at the highest-contributing loads would bring peak iTHD into compliant range.

**4. Outage event root cause review.** The 4 to 5 outage events observed across June, totaling an estimated 5 to 10 minutes, should be correlated against facility maintenance logs and utility event records. Repeated brief outages in a cold-chain environment carry compounding operational risk. If these are utility-origin events, power conditioning at the transformer service entrance warrants evaluation. If they are load-side events, protection coordination review is appropriate.

**5. Thermal burden trending.** The 602,911 BTU per hour thermal burden should be trended month-over-month as MPTS optimization progresses. Declining thermal burden confirms that reactive correction is translating into real heat relief — and provides the engineering team with a clear, measurable indicator of optimization progress independent of billing data.
